name: The Wild Service Tree of Moesgård
age_estimate: up to about 145 years (2010 register estimate)

location.address: Moesgård Museum park, east of the old manor buildings, Højbjerg, Aarhus

access: Free, in Moesgård's open park grounds (the museum building itself has paid entry; the surrounding park and forest are open to the public)
transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus to Moesgaard Museum, roughly 27-30 minutes, then a short walk into the park east of the manor buildings
verify_notes: Two Dansk Traeregister (DDF) submissions describe the same tree at identical coordinates (56.08711, 10.22860): Individual_ID=472 (reported by Hans Chr. Graversgaard, 2010, giving a 'maximal alder' of 145 years and calling it 'Formentlig Danmarks (og Europas) storste Tarmvrid-Ron', presumably Denmark's and Europe's largest wild service tree) and Individual_ID=1767 (re-surveyed by Hans Erik Lund, 2022: height 17.5m, girth 4.33m measured low at 0.3m because the tree forks into two-to-several stems from about 1m up, diameter 1.38m, status simply 'Levende' i.e. alive, legend repeats 'Danmarks tykkeste tarmvridron', Denmark's thickest). Treated here as ONE folded entry (register twin), not two trees. Danish Wikipedia's own article on Sorbus torminalis independently states 'Danmarks storste tarmvrid-ron vokser i parken bag den gamle hovedbygning pa Moesgard syd for Aarhus' (Denmark's largest wild service tree grows in the park behind the old main building at Moesgaard, south of Aarhus), which corroborates the register's superlative claim, though it may ultimately trace to the same original observation rather than being fully independent; flagged for that reason. Rated 'Bemaerkelsesvaerdig pa landsplan' (nationally noteworthy), the highest DDF tier. No fresh (post-2022) confirmation of vitality found this pass; the 2022 survey called it healthy. Remarkable fact for the writer: this is very likely the largest wild service tree in Denmark, a species that rarely grows this large anywhere in the country.

name: The Silver Fir by Moesgård's Small Cemetery

location.address: Moesgård Museum park, beside the small family cemetery on the park's eastern edge, Højbjerg, Aarhus

access: Free, in Moesgård's open park grounds (the museum building itself has paid entry; the surrounding park and forest are open to the public)
transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus to Moesgaard Museum, roughly 27-30 minutes, then a short walk into the park
verify_notes: Dansk Traeregister (Hans Erik Lund, 27-03-2022, GPS-verified): height 40.5m, girth 3.91m, diameter 1.24m, status 'Levende, sund' (alive, healthy), rated 'Kommunalt bemaerkelsesvaerdig' (municipally noteworthy, the register's lower tier). Register notes it stands 'pa den lille kirkegard' (on the small cemetery). AarhusWiki's detailed history of Moesgaard manor (citing the official 1997 Kommuneatlas Aarhus survey) independently confirms this cemetery exists: 'I parkens ostligste afgraensning ligger en lille gravplads omkranset af et stengaerde og beplantning' (In the park's easternmost boundary lies a small burial ground surrounded by a stone fence and planting), a private family burial ground begun in 1870 for the Dahl family who then owned Moesgaard, later receiving 14 graves moved from Aarhus's demolished Sondre Kirkegard in 1926. This corroborates the tree's location and the park's landscape character but does not independently confirm the tree's own species or measurements, hence flagged. No age given by any source; the 40.5m height is notable (a genuine giant for the species) but not verified against any national height-record list this pass. Age range here is a rough inference from girth, not a measurement; state as inferred, not documented, if used.

name: The Hornbeam of Moesgård

location.address: Moesgård Museum park, north side of the park's eastern end, Højbjerg, Aarhus

access: Free, in Moesgård's open park grounds (the museum building itself has paid entry; the surrounding park and forest are open to the public)
transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus to Moesgaard Museum, roughly 27-30 minutes, then a short walk into the park

Register's own note: 'Flot trae, men star lidt i skygge af nogle plataner' (a fine tree, but stands a little in the shade of some plane trees). No independent second source found this pass despite searching; a broader AarhusWiki history of Moesgaard's park (citing the 1997 Kommuneatlas survey) independently describes the eastern park as a landscape garden with 'fritstaende traeer' (free-standing trees), which is consistent context but not a per-tree confirmation. Flagged for single-source verification; no reason to doubt existence given the register's GPS-verified position and photo, but a second independent source should be sought in a future pass.

name: The Black Locust on Moesgård's Mound

location.address: Moesgård Museum park, on an artificial burial mound a few hundred metres east of the manor buildings, Højbjerg, Aarhus

access: Free, in Moesgård's open park grounds (the museum building itself has paid entry; the surrounding park and forest are open to the public)
transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus to Moesgaard Museum, roughly 27-30 minutes, then a short walk into the park
verify_notes: Single source: Dansk Traeregister (Hans Erik Lund, 27-03-2022, GPS-verified): height 15.5m, girth 4.98m (a large girth, but black locust grows fast so this does not imply great age), diameter 1.58m, status 'Levende, svag' (ALIVE but weak), rated 'Regionalt bemaerkelsesvaerdig'. Register's own legend: 'En stor del af kronen er dod, og traeet er svaekket af aelde' (a large part of the crown is dead, and the tree is weakened by age). Stands on what the register describes as a man-made burial mound (gravhoj), a folly-like landscape feature; a general AarhusWiki history of Moesgaard's park mentions the eastern landscape garden includes such romantic-period features though does not specifically name this mound. Delivered per the rule that a tree in decline still counts as alive; flag clearly that the most recent confirmation is from 2022 (about 4 years old) and the tree was already noted as weakening with significant crown dieback then, so a reader visiting today may find it further declined. No independent second source found for species/measurements.

name: The Happy Pig (Den Glade Gris)

location.address: Skåde Skov near Ørnereden, close to Moesgård, Højbjerg, Aarhus

access: Free, public forest (Skåde Skov / Moesgård Skov), open access
transport: Bus line 18 from central Aarhus towards Moesgaard Museum, then a walk into Skåde Skov towards Ørnereden (roughly 1.2km north of the main Moesgård tree cluster, along forest paths)
verify_notes: Single, thin source: Dansk Traeregister (reported by Gitte Aabo via email, 23-07-2020, GPS-verified position): species Fagus sylvatica, growth form 'Traee, forvredet-forkroeblet' (twisted-stunted growth), no height or girth recorded at all, rated 'Kommunalt bemaerkelsesvaerdig'. The nickname 'Den Glade Gris' (The Happy Pig) strongly suggests a locally-known landmark tree valued for its bizarre, twisted shape rather than for size or age, comparable to other Danish 'trold' or animal-shaped beeches from old grazing/pollarding. No independent second source found this pass; web searches for the name collided heavily with unrelated restaurants of the same name in Oslo and Copenhagen. Existence and location are register-documented with a verified GPS position, but nothing beyond that is confirmed. No age or size estimate is given here because there is no measurement to infer from; do not invent one. Flag prominently and consider this a strong candidate for a reader photo/description, since the visual is likely the whole story.

name: The Women's Oak of Viby (Kvindeegen)

location.address: Kirkevej, opposite the entrance to Viby Church's churchyard, Viby J, Aarhus

access: Free, open access, public roadside space opposite Viby Church
transport: Viby J station (Aarhus Letbane light rail and regional trains), short walk to Viby Church on Kirkevej
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree on the core story: in 1916 (AarhusWiki: to mark the constitutional change of 5 June 1915 that gave Danish women the vote) the Dansk Kvindesamfund's Viby branch planted this oak on land donated by Viby municipality, opposite the churchyard entrance at Viby Kirke. Dendron.dk (Knud Ib Christensen, 2008, GPS-verified): species Stilk-Eg (Quercus robur), status alive, rated 'Regionalt bemaerkelsesvaerdig'. DISCREPANCY worth flagging: the register's own age field says '110 ar (angiveligt plantet i 1916)' but its comment says 'Alderen er angivet for 2008' (the age is stated as of 2008) -- 2008 minus 1916 is only 92 years, not 110, so either the age field or the 2008 date-stamp is a register error (see the register-pitfall on corrupted fields). This entry uses the planting year 1916 as the anchor fact (independently corroborated by AarhusWiki's 'Kvindernes Eg' article) and gives today's (2026) age as roughly 110 years from that, rather than trusting the register's own age number. Historically significant per the qualifying bar even though only about a century old: a purpose-planted women's-suffrage memorial tree, a genre that exists in several Danish towns.

name: The Oak of Skåde

location.address: Roadside on Elmehøjvej, Skåde, Aarhus (protected since 1965)

access: Free, visible and reachable from the public road (Elmehøjvej); it stands at the roadside, not on private land
transport: Bus lines serving Skåde/Emiliedalsvej (e.g. 18 or 100) from central Aarhus, then roughly 10-15 minute walk along Elmehøjvej
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree: Dansk Traeregister (Hans Erik Lund, 14-06-2019, GPS-verified): 'Stilk-Eg' (Quercus robur), height 16m, girth 3.76m, diameter 1.2m, status alive, legend 'Fredet 1965' (protected 1965), rated 'Kommunalt bemaerkelsesvaerdig'. Denmark's official protected-nature register, fredninger.dk ('Skaade trae'), independently confirms: 'Et stort flot egetraee pa Elmehojvej i Skade er fredet' (a large, fine oak tree on Elmehojvej in Skade is protected), with driving directions ending 'her star egetraeet pa venstre side af vejen' (here the oak stands on the left side of the road), confirming it is a roadside tree rather than one set back on private land. No planting date or age given by either source; the age range here is a rough inference from girth for a slow-grown pedunculate oak, not a measurement, and should be presented as inferred. Protection dating to 1965 implies the tree was already considered a mature, valuable specimen six decades ago.
